explanation: Vector notation represents quantities with both magnitude and direction, distinguished from scalars (which have magnitude only), using bold letters, arrows, or column form.
key_concepts: Vector vs scalar quantities
Notation styles: bold, arrow, column
Zero vector

definitions.definition: A quantity possessing both magnitude and direction, represented as a, →AB, or a column of components.

formulas: Notation: a, or AB with arrow, or (x,y) as a column

worked_examples.problem: State whether speed and velocity are vectors or scalars
steps: Speed: magnitude only; Velocity: magnitude AND direction
worked_examples.answer: Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector

worked_examples.problem: Write the vector from A(2,3) to B(5,7) using arrow notation
steps: →AB represents displacement from A to B

practice_questions.q: Is mass a vector or scalar?
Is displacement a vector or scalar?
Is temperature a vector or scalar?
Is force a vector or scalar?
State the notation for the zero vector

exam_style_questions.q: Explain the difference between the vectors →AB and →BA.
exam_style_questions.answer: They have the same magnitude but opposite directions; →BA = -→AB

exam_style_questions.q: Give two real-world examples each of a vector and a scalar quantity, justifying your classification.
exam_style_questions.answer: Vectors: force (has direction and magnitude), velocity (speed with direction); Scalars: mass (magnitude only), time (magnitude only)

common_mistakes: Confusing vector notation with coordinate notation (they look similar but represent different things)
Forgetting that →AB and →BA are different (opposite direction) vectors
Treating a scalar quantity as if it had direction
tips: Always check whether a quantity has direction as well as magnitude to classify it as vector or scalar
→AB always means 'from A to B' — the order of letters matters and reverses the direction
Vectors can be represented multiple equivalent ways: bold letters, arrow notation, or column form
summary: Vector notation is the language for this entire category — correctly distinguishing vectors from scalars and understanding direction-sensitive notation is foundational.
quick_revision: Vector: magnitude AND direction; Scalar: magnitude only
→AB ≠ →BA (opposite directions)
Notation: bold a, arrow →AB, or column form

explanation: A column vector represents a vector's components as a vertical pair (or triple in 3D) of numbers, directly showing the horizontal and vertical displacement.
key_concepts: Component representation (x,y)
Relationship to Cartesian coordinates
Column vector arithmetic (add/subtract component-wise)

definitions.definition: A vector written as a vertical pair of components, e.g. (x above y), representing horizontal and vertical displacement.

formulas: Vector from A(x₁,y₁) to B(x₂,y₂): (x₂-x₁, y₂-y₁) as a column

worked_examples.problem: Write the column vector from A(1,2) to B(5,9)
Find the column vector representing 3 right, 2 down
steps: Right is positive x, down is negative y

practice_questions.q: Write the column vector from (0,0) to (6,-3)
Write the column vector from (2,5) to (2,9)
Write the column vector from (-1,-1) to (4,3)
State the column vector for 'stationary' (no movement)
Write the column vector from (7,2) to (1,2)

exam_style_questions.q: Given a=(3,-2) and b=(-1,5), find a+b and a-b as column vectors.
A vector (x,y) has the property that its column form equals the column vector from (2,3) to (2x-1, y+4). Find x and y.
exam_style_questions.answer: x=2x-1-2, so x=2x-3, x=3; y=y+4-3, so y=y+1, giving no solution unless reconsidering the setup — illustrates careful equation construction is needed for such problems

common_mistakes: Errors in the subtraction order when finding a column vector between two points (must be endpoint minus start point)
Sign errors, especially with negative components
Confusing a column vector with a coordinate point (they look similar but represent different concepts)
tips: Column vector from A to B is always (B's coordinates) minus (A's coordinates), component-wise
Keep track of signs carefully, especially when points have negative coordinates
Remember a column vector represents a displacement/direction, not a fixed position
summary: Column vectors provide the standard working notation for vector arithmetic throughout this category, directly connecting to coordinate geometry via component subtraction.
quick_revision: Vector A to B = (B-A) componentwise
Add/subtract vectors component-wise
Represents displacement, not a fixed position

explanation: Vector addition combines two vectors by adding their corresponding components, geometrically represented by placing vectors head-to-tail (the triangle or parallelogram rule).
key_concepts: Component-wise addition
Triangle rule (head-to-tail)
Parallelogram rule

definitions.definition: Combining two vectors by adding their corresponding components; geometrically, placing the tail of the second vector at the head of the first.

formulas: (a₁,a₂) + (b₁,b₂) = (a₁+b₁, a₂+b₂)

exam_style_questions.q: Given →AB=(3,5) and →BC=(2,-1), find →AC using the triangle rule for vector addition.
Three forces (2,3), (-1,4), and (x,y) act on a body such that the resultant is zero. Find x and y.

common_mistakes: Adding magnitudes instead of components when vectors aren't in the same direction
Sign errors when components are negative
Forgetting the triangle rule requires vectors to be placed head-to-tail, not tail-to-tail
tips: Always add corresponding components separately (x-components together, y-components together)
The triangle rule (→AB+→BC=→AC) is essential for combining displacement vectors along a path
Vector addition is commutative: a+b=b+a, matching the parallelogram rule's symmetry
summary: Vector addition is a fundamental operation combining component-wise arithmetic with the geometric triangle/parallelogram interpretation — essential for all further vector work.
quick_revision: Add corresponding components: (a₁+b₁, a₂+b₂)
Triangle rule: →AB+→BC=→AC
Vector addition is commutative

images.description: A diagram showing two vectors placed head-to-tail (triangle rule) with the resultant vector drawn from the start of the first to the end of the second, all labelled with arrows.
images.purpose: Visually demonstrates the triangle rule for vector addition, connecting the geometric and component-wise methods.

explanation: Vector subtraction combines a vector with the negative of another, found component-wise, and represents the displacement from one vector's endpoint to another's.
key_concepts: Component-wise subtraction
Relationship to addition of the negative vector
Geometric interpretation as displacement between two vectors' endpoints

definitions.definition: a - b = a + (-b), found by subtracting corresponding components.

formulas: (a₁,a₂) - (b₁,b₂) = (a₁-b₁, a₂-b₂)

worked_examples.problem: Subtract (2,7) - (5,3)
Given position vectors a=(1,2), b=(4,6), find →AB (which equals b-a)

exam_style_questions.q: Position vectors of A and B are a=(2,-1) and b=(6,7). Find →AB and →BA, and verify they are negatives of each other.
exam_style_questions.answer: →AB=b-a=(4,8); →BA=a-b=(-4,-8); confirmed →BA=-→AB

exam_style_questions.q: Given vectors p=(3,5) and q=(x,y) such that p-q=(1,2), find x and y.

common_mistakes: Subtracting in the wrong order (confusing a-b with b-a, which are negatives of each other)
Sign errors when components involve negative numbers
Forgetting that →AB = (position vector of B) - (position vector of A), not the other way round
tips: Always subtract component-wise, matching x with x and y with y
Remember →AB = b - a (position vector of the endpoint minus the start point) — a very common formula throughout vector geometry
a - b and b - a are negatives of each other, representing opposite directions
summary: Vector subtraction directly gives the displacement between two points via their position vectors, a formula (→AB=b-a) used constantly throughout vector geometry.
quick_revision: Subtract corresponding components
→AB = b - a (position vectors)
a-b and b-a are negatives (opposite directions)

explanation: Scalar multiplication scales a vector's magnitude by a real number, multiplying every component by that scalar, while preserving or reversing direction depending on the scalar's sign.
key_concepts: Multiplying every component by the scalar
Positive scalar preserves direction; negative reverses it
Scalar multiples are parallel to the original vector

definitions.definition: The operation ka, multiplying every component of vector a by the scalar k, scaling its magnitude and possibly reversing its direction.

formulas: k(a₁,a₂) = (ka₁, ka₂)

exam_style_questions.q: Given a=(3,4), find the vector 2a, and verify it has twice the magnitude but the same direction as a.
exam_style_questions.answer: 2a=(6,8); |a|=5, |2a|=10 (double); direction unchanged since the scalar is positive

exam_style_questions.q: Vectors p=(2,k) and q=(6,9) are parallel. Find k, using the fact that q=3p for some scalar relationship.
exam_style_questions.answer: If q is a scalar multiple of p: 6=3(2)✓ and 9=3k, so k=3

common_mistakes: Multiplying only one component by the scalar instead of both
Sign errors when the scalar is negative, forgetting it reverses the vector's direction
Confusing scalar multiplication (a number times a vector) with the dot product (a vector times a vector)
tips: Multiply EVERY component by the scalar — a very common source of error is forgetting one component
A negative scalar reverses the vector's direction (180° rotation) while a positive scalar preserves it
Any two parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other — this is the standard test for parallelism
summary: Scalar multiplication scales a vector's size and possibly flips its direction, and is the foundation for testing parallelism between vectors.
quick_revision: k(a₁,a₂) = (ka₁,ka₂)
k>0: same direction; k<0: opposite direction
Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other

explanation: The magnitude of a vector is its length, calculated using Pythagoras' Theorem applied to its components, giving a scalar (non-negative) value.
key_concepts: Pythagoras' Theorem applied to vector components
Magnitude notation |a|
Magnitude is always non-negative

definitions.definition: The length of a vector, calculated as |a| = √(a₁² + a₂²) for a vector (a₁,a₂).

formulas: |a| = √(a₁² + a₂²)

worked_examples.problem: Find the magnitude of (3,4)
Find the magnitude of (-5,12)

exam_style_questions.q: Given a=(2,k) has magnitude 2√5, find the possible values of k.
Find the magnitude of the vector 3a-2b, where a=(1,2) and b=(4,-1).

common_mistakes: Forgetting to square each component before adding (using components directly instead of squaring)
Sign errors leading to a negative value under the square root (shouldn't happen if squaring correctly)
Forgetting to take the final square root, leaving the answer as the sum of squares instead
tips: Magnitude is always the POSITIVE square root of the sum of squared components — never negative
This is exactly the distance formula from coordinate geometry, applied to vector components
Always simplify surds in the final magnitude where possible
summary: Magnitude quantifies a vector's length via Pythagoras' Theorem, connecting vectors directly to the distance formula from coordinate geometry.
quick_revision: |a| = √(a₁²+a₂²)
Always a non-negative value
Same formula as the distance formula in coordinate geometry

explanation: A unit vector has magnitude exactly 1, found by dividing a vector by its own magnitude, and is used to represent pure direction without regard to length.
key_concepts: Magnitude of a unit vector is always 1
Formula: divide vector by its magnitude
Standard unit vectors i and j

definitions.definition: A vector with magnitude exactly 1, obtained by dividing any vector by its own magnitude.

formulas: Unit vector of a = a / |a|

worked_examples.problem: Find the unit vector in the direction of (3,4)
Find the unit vector in the direction of (0,-7)

practice_questions.q: Find the unit vector in the direction of (6,8)
Find the unit vector in the direction of (5,0)
Find the unit vector in the direction of (-3,4)
Find the unit vector in the direction of (1,1)

exam_style_questions.q: Find a unit vector in the direction of a=(-8,15), and verify its magnitude equals 1.
A vector of magnitude 10 has the same direction as (3,4). Find this vector.
exam_style_questions.answer: Unit vector of (3,4) is (0.6,0.8); scale by 10: (6,8)

common_mistakes: Dividing only one component by the magnitude instead of both
Forgetting to find the magnitude first before dividing
Confusing a unit vector with the standard basis vectors i and j specifically (unit vectors can point in any direction)
tips: Always find |a| first, then divide EVERY component by this magnitude
A unit vector preserves the original direction exactly, only changing the length to 1
To find a vector of a specific length in a given direction, find the unit vector first, then scale by the desired length
summary: Unit vectors isolate pure direction from magnitude, a technique used throughout vector geometry, mechanics, and any context needing a specific-length vector in a given direction.
quick_revision: Unit vector = a / |a|
Always has magnitude exactly 1
Used to find a vector of any desired length in a given direction (scale the unit vector)

explanation: A position vector describes the location of a point relative to a fixed origin, providing the foundation for describing displacement, lines, and geometric relationships between points using vector algebra.
key_concepts: Position vector as displacement from the origin
Notation: often lowercase bold (a, b) for position vectors of A, B
Relationship between position vectors and displacement vectors

definitions.definition: The vector from the origin O to a specific point, representing that point's location.

formulas: Position vector of point A(x,y): a = (x,y)
→AB = b - a (displacement between two position vectors)

worked_examples.problem: State the position vector of the point (5,-2)
Given a=(1,3), b=(7,9), find →AB

practice_questions.q: Find the position vector of the midpoint of a=(2,4) and b=(8,10)
Given a=(5,1), find →AO (from A to origin)

exam_style_questions.q: Points A, B, C have position vectors a=(1,2), b=(5,8), c=(9,14). Show that A, B, C are collinear using vector methods.
exam_style_questions.answer: →AB=b-a=(4,6); →BC=c-b=(4,6); since →AB=→BC (same vector), A,B,C are collinear (in fact B is the midpoint of AC)

exam_style_questions.q: The midpoint M of AB has position vector m=(a+b)/2. Given a=(3,7) and m=(6,5), find b.

common_mistakes: Confusing a position vector (from the origin) with a general displacement vector (between two arbitrary points)
Errors in the formula →AB=b-a, sometimes reversing to a-b
Forgetting position vectors are tied to a fixed origin, unlike free vectors which can be translated anywhere
tips: A position vector always starts at the origin — this distinguishes it from a general displacement vector
Memorise →AB = b - a as one of the most frequently used vector formulas in geometry problems
The midpoint of AB has position vector (a+b)/2 — directly analogous to the coordinate midpoint formula
summary: Position vectors anchor points to a fixed origin, enabling displacement, midpoint, and ratio calculations throughout vector geometry using simple vector arithmetic.
quick_revision: Position vector: displacement from origin to the point
→AB = b - a
Midpoint of AB: (a+b)/2

explanation: A displacement vector describes the change in position from one point to another, distinct from a position vector (which is always measured from the origin), and can be found using position vector subtraction.
key_concepts: Displacement as change in position (not tied to origin)
Formula →AB=b-a using position vectors
Displacement vs distance (displacement includes direction)

definitions.definition: The vector representing the straight-line change in position from one point to another, found via →AB=b-a.

formulas: →AB = b - a, where a, b are position vectors of A, B

worked_examples.problem: Find the displacement from A(2,5) to B(9,1)
A particle moves from (0,0) to (3,4) then to (7,1). Find the total displacement.
steps: Total displacement = final position - initial position = (7,1)-(0,0)

practice_questions.q: A particle moves from (0,0) to (5,5) to (2,2). Find total displacement.
Find the magnitude of the displacement from (0,0) to (6,8)

exam_style_questions.q: A hiker walks from base camp with displacement (4,3)km, then a further displacement (-1,5)km. Find the hiker's total displacement from base camp, and their distance from base camp.
exam_style_questions.answer: Total displacement=(4-1,3+5)=(3,8)km; distance=|displacement|=√(9+64)=√73≈8.54km

exam_style_questions.q: Explain the difference between the total distance travelled and the magnitude of the total displacement for a journey that isn't a straight line, using a simple example.
exam_style_questions.answer: Total distance is the sum of all path lengths travelled (always ≥ the straight-line distance); displacement magnitude is the straight-line distance between start and end points only; e.g. walking 3km east then 3km west gives total distance 6km, but displacement is 0 (back at the start)

common_mistakes: Confusing displacement (net vector, straight-line) with total distance travelled (which can be much larger for a winding path)
Adding intermediate displacement vectors incorrectly when tracking a multi-step journey
Forgetting displacement is a vector (has direction), unlike distance which is a scalar
tips: For a multi-step journey, total displacement is simply final position minus initial position — you don't need to track every intermediate step for this specific value
Always distinguish displacement (vector, can be positive/negative/zero net effect) from distance (scalar, always positive, accumulates)
Use →AB=b-a directly whenever position vectors of the start and end points are known
summary: Displacement vectors capture net positional change, distinct from cumulative distance — an essential distinction throughout vector applications in geometry and mechanics.
quick_revision: →AB = b - a (final minus initial position)
Displacement ≠ distance (vector vs scalar, net vs cumulative)
For multi-step journeys, use only final and initial positions

explanation: Vector geometry uses vector algebra (addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication) to prove geometric properties such as parallelism, collinearity, and midpoints, offering an elegant alternative to coordinate or synthetic methods.
key_concepts: Proving parallelism via scalar multiples
Proving collinearity via shared direction vectors
Using vectors to establish geometric relationships in shapes

definitions.definition: A geometric proof using vector algebra (addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication) rather than coordinates or classical synthetic methods.

formulas: Parallel vectors: a = kb for some scalar k
Collinear points: →AB = k→BC for some scalar k

worked_examples.problem: Show that vectors (2,4) and (3,6) are parallel
worked_examples.answer: Parallel, since (3,6) is a scalar multiple of (2,4)

worked_examples.problem: Given position vectors a=(0,0), b=(4,6), c=(6,9), show A, B, C are collinear
worked_examples.answer: →BC is a scalar multiple of →AB, so A, B, C are collinear

practice_questions.q: Show that (1,2) and (2,5) are NOT parallel
practice_questions.answer: No scalar k satisfies both 2=k(1) and 5=k(2) simultaneously (k=2 from first, k=2.5 from second — inconsistent)

practice_questions.q: Given a=(1,1), b=(3,5), c=(5,9), determine if A,B,C are collinear
Find k such that (k,6) is parallel to (2,3)
Show OABC with position vectors o=(0,0), a=(3,0), b=(3,4), c=(0,4) forms a rectangle using vector methods
practice_questions.answer: →OA=(3,0), →CB=(3,0), so OA is parallel and equal to CB; →OC=(0,4), →AB=(0,4), so OC is parallel and equal to AB; opposite sides equal and parallel confirms a parallelogram; additionally →OA·→OC=0 confirms a right angle, making it a rectangle

exam_style_questions.q: OABC is a parallelogram with O the origin, a=→OA, and c=→OC. Express →OB and the position vector of the midpoint of AC in terms of a and c.
exam_style_questions.answer: →OB=a+c (diagonal of parallelogram); midpoint of AC has position vector (a+c)/2

exam_style_questions.q: Points P, Q, R have position vectors p=2i+3j, q=5i+7j, r=11i+15j. Determine if P, Q, R are collinear, showing full working.
exam_style_questions.answer: →PQ=q-p=3i+4j; →QR=r-q=6i+8j=2(3i+4j)=2→PQ; since →QR is a scalar multiple of →PQ, P,Q,R are collinear

common_mistakes: Not clearly demonstrating the scalar multiple relationship required to prove parallelism or collinearity
Confusing 'parallel' (same or opposite direction, not necessarily connected) with 'collinear' (lying on the same specific line)
Errors in vector subtraction when finding displacement vectors between points
tips: To prove collinearity, show that two displacement vectors sharing a common point (like →AB and →BC) are scalar multiples of each other
Parallel vectors just need to be scalar multiples — they don't need to share any point or lie on the same line
Vector methods are often more elegant and general than coordinate methods for proving properties like parallelograms and midpoints
summary: Vector geometry provides an elegant, general toolkit for proving classical geometric properties, with parallelism and collinearity as core building blocks for more complex proofs.
quick_revision: Parallel: a = kb for some scalar k
Collinear: →AB = k→BC for some scalar k (sharing point B)
Vector methods generalise well to proving shape properties (parallelograms, etc.)

explanation: Two vectors are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other, meaning they point in the same or exactly opposite direction, regardless of their individual magnitudes.
key_concepts: Scalar multiple test for parallelism
Same direction (positive scalar) vs opposite direction (negative scalar)
Application to proving geometric parallel lines

definitions.definition: Two vectors a and b are parallel if a = kb for some non-zero scalar k.

formulas: a is parallel to b if a = kb for some scalar k ≠ 0

worked_examples.problem: Determine if (6,9) and (2,3) are parallel
Determine if (4,-2) and (-2,1) are parallel

practice_questions.q: Find k such that (k,10) is parallel to (3,5)

exam_style_questions.q: Given a=(2,3) and b=(x,9), find x such that a and b are parallel, and state whether they point in the same or opposite direction.
exam_style_questions.answer: 9/3=3, so x=2×3=6; b=(6,9)=3a, same direction (positive scalar)

exam_style_questions.q: Vectors p=(3,k) and q=(k,12) are parallel. Find the possible values of k.
exam_style_questions.answer: 3/k=k/12 (cross-multiplying the parallel condition ratios); k²=36; k=±6

common_mistakes: Checking only one component's ratio and assuming parallelism without verifying the other component matches too
Confusing parallel (scalar multiple) with equal (identical vectors)
Sign errors when determining whether vectors point in the same or opposite direction
tips: Always verify BOTH components give the same scalar ratio — checking just one component isn't sufficient proof
A positive scalar multiple means same direction; negative means opposite direction (anti-parallel)
This test extends directly to proving lines are parallel in geometric vector proofs
summary: The scalar multiple test is the definitive, simple way to establish vector parallelism, foundational for geometric proofs throughout this category.
quick_revision: a parallel to b: a=kb for some scalar k
Check ALL components give the same ratio k
k>0: same direction; k<0: opposite direction

explanation: Points are collinear if the displacement vectors between consecutive pairs are scalar multiples of each other, indicating they all lie along the same straight line.
key_concepts: Testing via scalar multiple of displacement vectors
Sharing a common point (like B in →AB and →BC)
Distinguishing collinearity from mere parallelism

definitions.definition: Points A, B, C are collinear if →AB = k→BC (or equivalent) for some scalar k, meaning they share both direction AND a common point.

formulas: A, B, C collinear if →AB = k→BC for some scalar k

worked_examples.problem: Show A(1,1), B(3,5), C(4,7) are collinear
worked_examples.answer: Collinear, since →AB is a scalar multiple of →BC

worked_examples.problem: Show P(0,0), Q(2,3), R(5,8) are NOT collinear
steps: No consistent scalar k satisfies both ratios

practice_questions.answer: →AB=(1,1), →BC=(2,3), not a scalar multiple, not collinear

practice_questions.q: Find k such that (0,0), (k,3), (4,6) are collinear
practice_questions.answer: →AB=(k,3), →AC=(4,6)=2(2,3); for collinearity, (k,3) must be parallel to (4,6): k/4=3/6=0.5, k=2

exam_style_questions.q: Points A, B, C have position vectors a=3i-j, b=5i+3j, c=9i+11j. Determine whether A, B, C are collinear, and if so, find the ratio AB:BC.
exam_style_questions.answer: →AB=b-a=2i+4j; →BC=c-b=4i+8j=2(2i+4j)=2→AB; collinear, with AB:BC=1:2

exam_style_questions.q: Given that points with position vectors 2i+j, 5i+4j, and ki+10j are collinear, find k.
exam_style_questions.answer: →AB=3i+3j; →AC=(k-2)i+9j; for collinearity, →AC must be a scalar multiple of →AB: (k-2)/3=9/3=3; k-2=9; k=11

common_mistakes: Testing parallelism between vectors that don't share a common point, which only proves the LINES are parallel, not that all three points lie on one line
Sign or arithmetic errors when computing the displacement vectors
Forgetting to state the conclusion explicitly (collinear or not) after the calculation
tips: Always use displacement vectors that share a common point (like →AB and →BC, sharing point B) to correctly test collinearity, not just parallelism
Once collinearity is established, the scalar k found also gives the ratio in which the points divide the line
State your conclusion clearly: 'since →AB is a scalar multiple of →BC, A, B, C are collinear'
summary: Collinearity testing via vectors requires displacement vectors sharing a common point — this is subtly different from (and stronger than) simple parallelism testing.
quick_revision: Use →AB and →BC (sharing point B)
Collinear if →AB = k→BC for some scalar k
The scalar k also reveals the division ratio along the line

explanation: Vector ratios describe how a point divides a line segment between two other points, expressed using position vectors and the section formula generalised to vector form.
key_concepts: Section formula in vector form
Internal division ratios
Relationship to the coordinate section formula

definitions.definition: For point P dividing AB in ratio m:n, the position vector p = (na + mb)/(m+n).

formulas: p = (n·a + m·b) / (m+n), for P dividing AB in the ratio m:n (from A to B)

worked_examples.problem: Find the position vector of P dividing AB in ratio 2:3, given a=(0,0), b=(10,15)
Find the position vector of the midpoint of a=(2,4), b=(8,10)

practice_questions.q: Find P dividing AB (a=(0,0), b=(6,12)) in ratio 1:2
Find P dividing AB (a=(2,2), b=(10,10)) in ratio 3:1
Find the midpoint of a=(1,1), b=(7,9)
Find P dividing AB (a=(-2,4), b=(6,-4)) in ratio 3:5
Find P dividing AB (a=(1,1), b=(5,9)) in ratio 1:3

exam_style_questions.q: Points A and B have position vectors a=4i+2j and b=10i+14j. Point P divides AB such that AP:PB=1:2. Find the position vector of P.
Point P has position vector p=(3a+2b)/5. Explain what ratio P divides AB in.
exam_style_questions.answer: Comparing to p=(n·a+m·b)/(m+n), here n=3, m=2, so AP:PB=m:n=2:3

common_mistakes: Mixing up which ratio value (m or n) corresponds to which endpoint in the formula
Forgetting the formula's structure has n (not m) multiplying a, and m (not n) multiplying b — easily reversed
Arithmetic errors when combining the vector components
tips: Double-check which point the ratio starts from (A to B) — this determines which value is m and which is n in the formula
The vector section formula is the direct vector-algebra equivalent of the coordinate section formula covered in Coordinate Geometry
Simplify all vector components fully at each step to avoid arithmetic errors
summary: Vector ratios generalise the midpoint formula, providing a systematic way to find any point dividing a segment in a given ratio, purely through vector algebra.
quick_revision: p = (n·a+m·b)/(m+n) for P dividing AB in ratio m:n
Midpoint is the special case m:n=1:1
Double-check which value is m vs n

explanation: The midpoint of a line segment joining two points can be found directly using their position vectors, averaging the vectors component-wise, exactly mirroring the coordinate midpoint formula.
key_concepts: Averaging position vectors
Special case of the vector ratio formula (ratio 1:1)
Applications in vector geometry proofs

definitions.definition: The position vector of the midpoint M of AB is m = (a+b)/2, where a, b are the position vectors of A, B.

worked_examples.problem: Find the midpoint of a=(2,6), b=(8,2)
Given midpoint m=(4,4) and a=(1,7), find b

practice_questions.q: Find the midpoint of a=(0,0), b=(6,10)

exam_style_questions.q: Prove using vectors that the line joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half its length (the Midpoint Theorem).
exam_style_questions.answer: Let triangle have vertices with position vectors a, b, c; midpoint of AB: (a+b)/2; midpoint of AC: (a+c)/2; vector between these midpoints: (a+c)/2-(a+b)/2=(c-b)/2=(1/2)(c-b)=(1/2)→BC; this shows the midpoint-joining segment is parallel to BC and exactly half its length

definitions.definition: The point (if any) where two vector-defined lines meet, found by solving for parameter values making both equations agree.
